CE/CNEE Predictions vs. UCSC mm39 35-way Conserved Elements

Question

Our phastCons-derived CEs (04-phastcons/regions) and CNEEs (05-cnees/phastcons/bed/*.cnees.bed4) come from a 15-species Cactus alignment. As an independent sanity check, how well do they agree with UCSC’s mm39-35way.bed - conserved elements called from a completely different, much larger (35-species) multiz alignment, using a completely different pipeline (phastCons on multiz, not Cactus)? Agreement here isn’t proof of correctness, but strong disagreement would be a red flag; strong agreement is a meaningful, independent corroboration of what our pipeline is finding. This also compares our two split_strategy runs (num_seqs, now the default, and ns, from [[resource-usage-and-defaults.Rmd]]’s comparison) against this same external reference, and, separately, compares cnees_from_conserved_chr’s old CDS-subtract/fragment-split behavior against its new drop-entire-CE-on-any-CDS-overlap behavior (see “CNEE definition change” below) using two runs (num_seqs, num_seqs_no_overlap) that are identical in every other config setting.

Methodology

Our reference (GCA_000001635.9) is the exact same assembly as UCSC’s mm39/GRCm39 - confirmed directly from the FASTA header (“GRCm39 reference primary assembly”), the reference GFF’s filename, and NCBI’s own sequence_report.tsv for this assembly. Same assembly means same coordinates - no liftover needed, only a chromosome-name translation (UCSC’s chr1 etc. to GenBank accessions like CM000994.3), via translate_ucsc_chroms.sh in this directory (reusing the header-lookup awk idiom already used for exactly this in the support data repo’s 04_replace_bed_seqids_with_genbank.sh), restricted to the 21 real chromosomes this pipeline actually has predictions for.

Per chromosome, per run (num_seqs, ns, num_seqs_no_overlap), per our-track (CE, CNEE), compare_to_ucsc.py runs bedtools jaccard and bedtools intersect (via bedtools-env’s bedtools, called by absolute path rather than conda activate - this session hit a real bug twice where conda activate doesn’t reliably win on $PATH) between our bed and the translated UCSC bed for that chromosome, producing ucsc-comparison-flat.tsv.

A real pipeline quirk surfaced and worked around while building this: the raw CE bed (04-phastcons/regions) uses phastCons’s own truncated chromosome name (e.g. CM000994, no version suffix) rather than the full accession every other output uses - the same thing cnees_from_conserved_chr already has to normalize internally when reading this same file to build CNEEs. compare_to_ucsc.py does the same normalization before comparing. Relatedly, the on-disk 04-phastcons/regions/{group}/{chrom}.bed file sits next to a same-named {chrom}/ directory (holding run_phastcons_chr’s small chunks.done/global_rho.txt bookkeeping files, left behind after cleanup_chunk_intermediates removes the real per-chunk outputs) - not a bug, but an easy thing to overlook browsing the output tree.

For the CNEE track specifically, UCSC’s track has no CDS subtracted while ours does, so the raw comparison undersells the real agreement. compare_to_ucsc.py also computes a fairer variant (cnee_vs_nocds_ucsc): bedtools subtract-ing our own per-chromosome CDS bed (05-cnees/phastcons/bed/*.cds.bed, already produced by extract_cds_bed_chr from the same reference GFF - no new CDS extraction needed) from the UCSC bed before comparing.

Separately, compare_to_atac.py checks how often each track (our CE/CNEE, all three runs, and UCSC’s raw CE) overlaps an independent ATAC-seq peak set - skin, late anagen (GSM4156597_skin.late.anagen.peaks.mm39.bed, translated the same way), producing atac-comparison-flat.tsv.

  • Data source: data/hamsters/workflow-tests/test-full-split-aln/ (num_seqs) and data/hamsters/workflow-tests/test-full-gc/ (ns), the same two real, full 21-chromosome runs already compared to each other in resource-usage-and-defaults.Rmd; plus data/hamsters/workflow-tests/test-no-overlap/ (num_seqs_no_overlap) - a third real, full 21-chromosome run with the exact same config as num_seqs (split_strategy: num_seqs, rho_mode: fixed, fixed_rho: 0.3, cnee_ces_merge_gap_bp: 5, cnee_min_len_bp: 50 - confirmed identical from each run’s own summary_report.html) except that it was run after cnees_from_conserved_chr’s CDS-overlap handling changed from subtract-and-keep-fragments to drop-the-whole-CE, isolating the effect of that one algorithm change.
  • UCSC track: mm39-35way.bed (/n/holylfs05/LABS/informatics/Everyone/support/20251114-raftrey-hamster-wga/data/bed/), 4,829,248 elements genome-wide; 4,826,807 fall within our 21 target chromosomes after translation.
  • 189 rows (21 chromosomes x 3 runs x 3 tracks - ce, cnee, cnee_vs_nocds_ucsc) in ucsc-comparison-flat.tsv; 147 rows (21 chromosomes x 7 sources - 3 runs x 2 tracks plus ucsc_ce) in atac-comparison-flat.tsv.

Overlap: CE and CNEE vs. UCSC, num_seqs vs. ns

This section is scoped to the two split_strategy runs (num_seqs, ns) only - num_seqs_no_overlap (same split_strategy, different CDS-overlap handling) is compared separately in “CNEE definition change” below, to keep the two independent axes of comparison from being conflated in the same plot.

Aggregate overlap vs. UCSC mm39 35-way, summed across all 21 chromosomes
our_run our_track n_chroms total_bp_ours total_bp_ucsc total_bp_intersect mean_jaccard pct_ours_in_ucsc pct_ucsc_in_ours
ns ce 21 140939708 150673314 78625691 0.356 55.8 52.2
num_seqs ce 21 139193307 150673314 79473312 0.364 57.1 52.7
ns cnee 21 86119768 150673314 48841475 0.250 56.7 32.4
num_seqs cnee 21 91245906 150673314 51418308 0.259 56.4 34.1

Both our CE and CNEE sets overlap the independent UCSC track substantially above zero across every chromosome, and the pattern is consistent with what’s already known about this alignment: CM001014.3 (the poorly cross-species-aligned xy scaffold flagged earlier this session) shows dramatically lower agreement (Jaccard ~0.04-0.06) than every other chromosome (~0.2-0.44) - the independent UCSC track corroborates that this specific chromosome’s alignment quality problem is real, not an artifact of our own pipeline.

CE overlap is consistently a bit higher than CNEE overlap for both runs - expected, since UCSC’s track (like our raw CEs) includes coding regions, while our CNEEs have already had CDS subtracted out. The next section quantifies exactly how much of that gap is just the CDS-inclusion difference versus a real disagreement.

A fairer CNEE comparison: subtracting CDS from UCSC’s track too

This section includes all three runs (num_seqs, ns, num_seqs_no_overlap) - unlike “Overlap” and “Scale” above, it isn’t scoped to the split-strategy comparison.

CNEEs vs. UCSC’s raw track vs. UCSC with our own CDS bed subtracted first
our_run our_track mean_jaccard pct_ours_in_ucsc pct_ucsc_in_ours
ns cnee 0.250 56.7 32.4
ns cnee_vs_nocds_ucsc 0.291 56.7 39.3
num_seqs cnee 0.259 56.4 34.1
num_seqs cnee_vs_nocds_ucsc 0.302 56.4 41.4
num_seqs_no_overlap cnee 0.247 56.0 32.2
num_seqs_no_overlap cnee_vs_nocds_ucsc 0.287 56.0 39.0

Subtracting CDS from UCSC’s track before comparing raises agreement for all three runs (mean Jaccard: num_seqs 0.259 -> 0.302, ns 0.250 -> 0.291, num_seqs_no_overlap 0.247 -> 0.287) - confirming the CE/CNEE gap above is partly, not entirely, a CDS-inclusion artifact rather than a real difference in what the two pipelines find non-coding-conserved. num_seqs_no_overlap’s gap (0.040) is only marginally smaller than num_seqs’s (0.042), even though its CNEEs never have CDS in them at all under the new definition - most of the remaining gap is better explained by scale (UCSC calling more, shorter elements; see “Scale” below) than by CDS-inclusion, under either CNEE definition.

Scale: element counts and lengths

Element counts and mean length: ours (both strategies, both tracks) vs. UCSC
our_run our_track total_n_ours mean_len_ours_bp
ns ce 2127094 66.3
ns cnee 575157 149.7
num_seqs ce 1554862 89.5
num_seqs cnee 592809 153.9
- ucsc (per-chrom total) 4826807 31.2

UCSC’s 35-way track calls roughly 2-3x more elements than either of our runs on the same chromosomes, consistent with it being built from a much deeper (35 vs 15 species) alignment - more species generally means more statistical power to detect shorter/weaker conservation signals. This scale difference is the main reason absolute overlap percentages sit around 25-40% rather than higher: a majority of UCSC’s smaller/weaker elements simply aren’t things a shallower alignment could ever call in the first place, independent of any real disagreement.

CNEE definition change: drop-on-overlap vs. subtract-and-split

cnees_from_conserved_chr used to turn a conserved element (CE) into one or more CNEE candidates by subtracting CDS from it - a CDS in the middle of a CE split it into two flanking fragments, and a CDS clipping just one end left the non-overlapping remainder. It now instead drops the entire CE if it overlaps a CDS at all, no matter how - fully contained, split in the middle, or clipped at one end - so only CEs with zero CDS overlap become CNEE candidates. num_seqs (old behavior) and num_seqs_no_overlap (new behavior) are otherwise identical runs (see Data source above), isolating this one change.

CE -> CNEE-candidate funnel totals (before cnee_min_len_bp), old vs. new CDS-overlap handling
run total_ces_raw total_ces_merged total_candidates pct_of_merged
num_seqs 1554862 1529874 1576531 103.0
num_seqs_no_overlap 1554867 1529868 1287232 84.1
Final CNEE set (after the cnee_min_len_bp length filter), old vs. new CDS-overlap handling
our_run total_n total_bp mean_len_bp
num_seqs 592809 91245906 153.9
num_seqs_no_overlap 564824 86480567 153.1

Genome-wide, the new definition keeps 18.4% fewer CNEE candidates (1,287,232 vs. 1,576,531) before the length filter, but only 6.7% less total bp (106.2 vs. 113.8 Mbp) - most of the count drop is fragments that only existed because the old behavior split one CE into two at every internal CDS, not new bp actually being excluded. The funnel table above makes this concrete: the old definition’s candidate count is 103.0% of the merged CE count - mathematically impossible under the new definition, which can only ever keep a CE whole or drop it, never turn one CE into more than one candidate. The new definition’s 84.1% is the first cnee_after_cds_drop-stage number that’s guaranteed to be <= 100% by construction. After the length filter, the gap narrows further (4.7% fewer elements, 5.2% less bp) since many of the short flanking fragments the old behavior produced wouldn’t have passed cnee_min_len_bp anyway. The new definition is stricter - every surviving CNEE is guaranteed to have zero CDS overlap at all, rather than “the non-coding part of a CE that touched a CDS somewhere” - at a modest cost in yield.

Does the new, stricter definition need less of a boost from CDS-subtracting UCSC’s track, since its CNEEs never have CDS in them to begin with? See “A fairer CNEE comparison” above, which covers all three runs together - the short answer is only marginally, since most of the remaining CE/CNEE-vs-UCSC gap is better explained by scale than by CDS-inclusion.

Overlap with an independent ATAC-seq peak set

How often do CEs/CNEEs from either UCSC or our own pipeline land in independently accessible chromatin - skin, late anagen ATAC-seq peaks (GSM4156597_skin.late.anagen)?

ATAC-seq peak overlap by element count, Jaccard, and bp fraction - summed across all 21 chromosomes
source total_n_elements total_n_overlapping pct_elements_overlapping mean_jaccard pct_elements_bp_in_atac
ns_cnee 575157 117759 20.47 0.0734 15.91
num_seqs_cnee 592809 121015 20.41 0.0742 15.55
num_seqs_no_overlap_cnee 564824 112810 19.97 0.0694 15.05
ns_ce 2127094 308182 14.49 0.0841 14.21
num_seqs_ce 1554862 252102 16.21 0.0834 14.16
num_seqs_no_overlap_ce 1554867 252100 16.21 0.0834 14.16
ucsc_ce 4826807 549865 11.39 0.0605 10.07

Three different ways of asking “how much overlap” tell a fuller story together, and don’t all agree on the same ranking. By bp fraction and by element count, our CNEEs (all three runs, ~15-16% of bp, ~20-20.5% of elements) lead raw CEs (~14.2%, ~14.5-16.2%), which lead UCSC’s raw track (~10.1%, ~11.4%) - CNEEs aren’t just bp-heavier where they overlap, more of them overlap at all. Jaccard breaks that ranking: raw CEs (~0.083-0.084) are actually higher than CNEEs (~0.069-0.074), both well above UCSC (~0.061). This isn’t a contradiction - Jaccard penalizes union size, and CEs (larger, includes coding regions) vs. CNEEs (smaller, non-coding only) trade off differently against a fixed-size ATAC peak set than bp-fraction or count-overlap do; the bp/count metrics answer “of what we predicted, how much lands in a peak”, while Jaccard also punishes predicting territory ATAC doesn’t touch. All three metrics agree that UCSC’s much larger, shorter-element track (see “Scale” above) ranks lowest on every measure.

num_seqs_no_overlap’s CNEEs (new, drop-on-overlap definition) overlap ATAC peaks at a slightly lower rate than num_seqs’s (old, subtract/split definition) on every metric - 19.97% vs. 20.41% of elements, 15.05% vs. 15.55% of bp, 0.069 vs. 0.074 Jaccard. The difference is small and the ranking among all sources is unchanged either way; it isn’t strong enough evidence on its own to say whether the CEs the new definition drops for CDS overlap were disproportionately near regulatory (ATAC-accessible) sequence, or whether this is just noise from a modestly smaller element set.

Our CNEEs overlap ATAC peaks at a modestly higher rate than our raw CEs, for both strategies - consistent with CDS-subtraction concentrating CNEEs toward non-coding, potentially regulatory sequence rather than diluting them with coding regions that aren’t enriched for this specific tissue’s accessible chromatin. UCSC’s much larger, shorter-element track shows the lowest overlap rate of the five, consistent with the “Scale” section above - a large fraction of its elements are short, weak calls that a shallower alignment (ours) or a specific regulatory assay (ATAC) wouldn’t independently flag either.

Caveats

  • Not a ground truth. UCSC’s 35-way track is itself a phastCons call on a different alignment, not an experimentally validated set of true conserved elements - agreement is corroborating evidence, not a correctness proof, and disagreement doesn’t necessarily mean either pipeline is wrong. The same applies to the ATAC-seq comparison in the other direction: it’s one tissue, one timepoint - absence of overlap there doesn’t mean an element isn’t real or isn’t regulatory in some other context.
  • mm39-35way.bed’s score/lod columns were not used for any filtering - the full track is compared as-is. A confidence-filtered subset might show tighter agreement.
  • The phastCons chrom-name-truncation quirk (see Methodology) affects only the raw CE bed; if any future consumer of 04-phastcons/regions/*.bed reads it directly by chrom name without normalizing, it will silently fail the same way this analysis initially did.
  • CM001014.3 has zero ATAC-seq peaks in the source dataset entirely (not specific to our pipeline or UCSC) - excluded from the ATAC plot above for that reason, not because of any predicted-element issue.
